processing: Not a leaf style: a very large amount of ordinary black tea is brewed or boiled down in a small volume of water for a long time, sometimes overnight.
harvest_season: Not tied to a harvest; made from whatever black tea is available.
appearance_dry: Ordinary loose black tea or tea bags, in quantity.
appearance_liquor: Nearly black and opaque, as is to be expected from such a concentration.
appearance_wet: A dense sodden mass of dark leaf settled at the bottom of the mug.
taste_profile: Extremely bitter and harsh. It is sipped slowly, traditionally with something salty such as salted fish, and sometimes with sugar.

brewing.notes: Recorded for what it is, not as a recommendation. Fifty grams or more to a small mug is the classic description, and gulping it can cause vomiting. It is sipped in small amounts.

vintage_note: Never sold as a product, by year or by season. It is brewed on the spot from cheap black tea.
description:
Chifir is tea taken as far as it will go: a mug with so much black tea in it that it becomes a stimulant. It belongs to the Soviet and post-Soviet prison world, and also, in the accounts of writers, to long-distance drivers and others working in the far north.

The method is simple. Pour boiled water over several tablespoons of leaf per person, or boil it down, and leave it, sometimes all night. In cells it has been made on hot plates, with improvised heating elements or over burning rags and paper. A weaker version is known as kupchik or kupets.

It is very bitter and is sipped rather than drunk, since gulping it can make you sick. People take it hot or cold, and Shalamov's description has it followed with salted fish.

This entry is here for its cultural history rather than as a suggestion for the tea table. Nobody buys it, and there is no good version to seek out.
history:
The origin of the word is uncertain. Suggestions include chikhir, a strong Caucasian wine or a Siberian word for spoiled wine; chagir, a tea substitute from Eastern Siberia; and a Mongolian word for sweetness.

Its documented life is largely literary and comes from memoirs of detention. Varlam Shalamov's Kolyma Tales describe it as a northern drink that drives away sleep, prized by criminals and by drivers on long hauls, and it appears in Sergei Dovlatov, Anatoly Marchenko, Mikhail Demin and Oleg Kuvaev too. Irina Ratushinskaya recalls brewing it as a banned activity among prisoners in her memoir Grey Is the Colour of Hope.
